title: The Global Smartphone Market Is Heading for Its Steepest Annual Contraction on Record. Budget Phones Under $150 May Disappear Entirely.
excerpt: Counterpoint Research now projects a 13.9 per cent decline in 2026 shipments to 1.08 billion units. The memory chip shortage, worsened by the Iran war, is killing the low end of the market while Apple and Samsung pull further ahead.
body:
The global smartphone market is heading for its worst year on record. Counterpoint Research, an independent firm that publishes quarterly shipment data, said on Monday that worldwide smartphone shipments are projected to fall 13.9 per cent this year to 1.08 billion units — the steepest annual decline the industry has ever recorded.

The forecast is a downgrade from the 12.4 per cent decline Counterpoint projected in February. The deterioration is being driven by a worsening shortage of memory chips, exacerbated by the ongoing war between the United States and Iran, which has disrupted energy supplies and added cost pressure across the semiconductor supply chain.

The Budget End Is Getting Crushed

The impact is being felt most acutely at the lower end of the market. As chipmakers redirect production capacity toward AI-related chips — where margins are substantially higher — the economics of producing entry-level smartphones are collapsing. Memory chips that once went into budget handsets are being allocated to data centre hardware, AI accelerators, and high-end consumer electronics instead.

Global smartphone wholesale prices rose 14 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 while shipments fell 3.1 per cent year on year. That divergence is expected to widen as pre-shortage inventory is depleted. Counterpoint warns that some smartphone models priced below $150 may disappear from the market entirely.

"Smartphone makers in the low and mid-tier are caught between cost increases they cannot absorb and consumers with limited spending power," said Wang Yang, a principal analyst at Counterpoint. "The question is no longer how to grow shipments or market share, but whether to remain in the market at all."

What This Means for Indian Brands

The contraction is particularly consequential for Indian smartphone brands and the Indian consumer market. India is the world's second-largest smartphone market by volume, and the sub-$150 segment — the one under the greatest threat — accounts for a significant share of domestic sales. Brands like Xiaomi, Realme, Vivo, and Samsung's budget lines have built their Indian market positions on affordable devices powered by commodity memory and mid-range processors.

If those components become scarce or prohibitively expensive, the brands have limited options: raise prices and lose volume, or absorb costs and lose margins. Neither path is sustainable for long.

For consumers in India, the practical effect is that the next phone upgrade will be more expensive than the last one, and the gap between a budget device and a flagship will narrow — not because budget phones are getting better, but because they are getting more expensive to make.

The Winners: Apple and Samsung

At the top of the market, the picture is different. Apple and Samsung, which source components through long-term contracts and can absorb temporary margin pressure, are expected to outperform the broader market. Samsung's recent announcement that it has begun shipping 12-layer HBM4E memory samples — the next generation of high-bandwidth memory used in AI processors — signals that the company is prioritising its most profitable product lines.

For Apple, which reported record iPhone revenue in its most recent quarter, the chip shortage has created an unusual competitive advantage. Its vertically integrated supply chain, including custom-designed chips manufactured by TSMC under preferential allocation agreements, insulates it from the worst of the component crunch. Consumers who might have considered a mid-range Android device are increasingly trading up to an iPhone because the price gap has narrowed while the availability gap has widened.

The Investment Angle for NRI Portfolios

For NRI investors with exposure to technology stocks, the smartphone contraction creates a bifurcated landscape. Companies tied to premium devices and AI infrastructure — Apple, Samsung, TSMC, and to some extent Qualcomm's premium Snapdragon line — are relatively insulated. Companies tied to volume shipments in emerging markets face earnings pressure.

Indian IT services firms like Infosys, TCS, and Wipro are indirectly affected. A smartphone contraction in India slows the growth of digital services, fintech adoption, and e-commerce — all categories that Indian IT firms serve.

The memory chip shortage itself is a double-edged trade. SK Hynix and Samsung's memory divisions are seeing margins expand as prices rise, but the volume decline limits revenue upside. Micron Technology, whose shares jumped more than 5 per cent in pre-market trading on Monday following Nvidia's AI laptop announcements, is benefiting from the AI side of the demand equation while watching the consumer side contract.

The Bigger Picture

The smartphone industry's record contraction is not just a supply-chain story. It is a structural shift. The AI boom is fundamentally reallocating semiconductor capacity away from consumer electronics and toward data centres and enterprise infrastructure. For the first time, the smartphone — the device that defined the last fifteen years of technology — is being deprioritised by the companies that make its components.

That reallocation will not reverse quickly. New semiconductor fabrication plants take three to five years to build and commission. The capacity that is being redirected toward AI today will not return to consumer electronics until the economics change — and there is no sign that they will.

For consumers, particularly in price-sensitive markets like India, the implication is clear: the era of steadily improving, steadily cheaper smartphones is ending. The next generation of devices will cost more, do more, and be produced in smaller quantities. The budget phone, as millions in the developing world have known it, may be approaching its last chapter.
